lessons.title: Understanding how a business works
lessons.html:
The business behind the hunt

Whether you work for a hunting outfitter, a game lodge or a farm, you work in a business. Understanding how it makes money, what it costs and how your work affects results makes you more valuable and prepares you to run your own business one day.

Forms of business

  • Sole proprietor: one owner, simple, but the owner is personally liable for debts.
  • Partnership: two or more owners share profits and liability.
  • Private company (Pty) Ltd: a separate legal person registered with CIPC under the Companies Act 71 of 2008; owners' liability is limited.
  • Co-operative: members own and control it together, common in agriculture.

Functions of a business

FunctionIn a hunting operation
Marketing and salesShows, website, agents, quotes
OperationsHunts, accommodation, trophy handling
FinanceBudgets, invoices, payments, tax
Human resourcesStaff, contracts, training
Administration and compliancePermits, registers, licences, records

Income, costs and profit

Profit = income − expenses. Example for a seven-day hunt:

ItemAmount (R)
Income: daily rates and trophy fees120 000
Costs: trophy animals' value to landowner, staff, food, fuel, permits85 000
Profit before overheads and tax35 000

The business also has fixed costs (salaries, insurance, vehicle finance) that must be paid even when there are no clients, so the season must earn enough to cover the quiet months.

lessons.title: Your role, rules and good business practice
lessons.html:
How your work affects the business

  • Quality: a well-run hunt brings repeat clients and referrals.
  • Cost control: careful use of fuel, ammunition, food and equipment saves money.
  • Time: punctuality keeps the programme running.
  • Reputation: one unethical or unsafe act can damage the business for years.

Laws a business must follow

  • Registration with CIPC for companies; registration with SARS for income tax and, if turnover is above the threshold, VAT.
  • Labour laws: Basic Conditions of Employment Act 75 of 1997, Labour Relations Act 66 of 1995, UIF and COIDA registration.
  • Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993.
  • Consumer Protection Act 68 of 2008 and POPIA (Act 4 of 2013) for clients.
  • Industry laws: provincial hunting permits, Firearms Control Act 60 of 2000, Biodiversity Act TOPS permits.

Business documents

  • Quotation: what will be provided and at what price.
  • Contract or booking confirmation: terms, deposit, cancellation policy.
  • Invoice: request for payment.
  • Receipt: proof of payment.
  • Records: hunting registers, stock lists, staff time sheets.

Keep documents for the period required by law; SARS can ask to see them.

Ethics in business

Be honest with clients about prices, game availability and trophy quality. Never accept bribes or take part in illegal hunts or the sale of wildlife products without permits. Treat staff fairly.

Planning and growth

A simple business plan describes the product, the market, competitors, the team, the finances and the goals. Review it each year. Look for new opportunities, such as adding photographic safaris in the off-season or offering venison products.

Key points

  • Businesses can be sole proprietors, partnerships, companies or co-operatives.
  • Profit is income minus expenses; fixed costs continue in quiet months.
  • Your quality, cost control and reputation affect the bottom line.
  • Comply with tax, labour, safety, consumer and industry laws.
  • Use proper documents and act ethically.
